reasoning_traces.think:
The core insight is that estimation risk in Kelly investing arises from mis-specification of drift (u,d,p). The authors propose hedging via European puts, but show that in the absence of such instruments, a convex mixture of Kelly strategies—each optimized under different beliefs—achieves the same asymptotic growth rate as the best individual strategy. This is formalized in Theorem 4.1, which states that the asymptotic growth rate of the mixture equals the maximum of its components’ growth rates. In practice, this means that even if the true parameters are unknown, one can construct a portfolio that asymptotically performs as well as the best possible belief-based strategy. The key innovation lies in replacing stochastic option positions with deterministic convex combinations of model variants—a computationally tractable alternative. The failure mode occurs at finite n, where the mixture does not dominate individual strategies globally, especially in short horizons. Thus, while the theoretical guarantee is strong, practical deployment requires careful calibration of the mixture weights and awareness of finite-sample limitations.
